title: Lag watchdog: names the process behind a freeze and offers to end it
detail: New apps/watchdog (vitals-watchdog.exe, ~3 MB, HKCU Run, no admin). Tick 1 s: CPU >= 90 % or Normal-priority probe woken >= 40 ms late, 5 of 8 bad ticks = episode; memory load >= 95 %; foreground IsHungAppWindow 5 s outranks both. Blame walks DOWN subtrees to the smallest carrying 70 % of load; shells/terminals/IDEs/service hosts transparent; parent link only if parent started first (PID reuse). Never offered: hosts with children, session chain (explorer/svchost/winlogon...), non-Safe assess_termination, protected (ProcessProtectionLevelInfo), already below-normal. Toast (Alarm scenario so it breaks through Do Not Disturb) with End [+children], Lower priority (whole tree), Ignore 30 min; clicks honoured only for pending keys < 15 min; End re-reads the tree, children first, each via terminate (start-time + critical re-check), UAC retry for another user's process. Main thread TIME_CRITICAL in a Normal-class process. EN+RO strings. Root cause of the incident fixed separately: run-build.ps1 now runs builds BelowNormal

title: CI: the vitals-win suite can neither hang (crash dump tests) nor crash (WinRT on a torn-down apartment); every CI and release job has a timeout
detail: (1) Rust test (windows) hung after crash_child ... ok on 07b011d (75 min) and 8059efe attempt 1 (40 min): the two writer tests called MiniDumpWriteDump on the test binary itself while ~16 tests ran in parallel. Every dump is now written by a child running one test on one thread (--exact, --test-threads=1, stdio null, 60 s kill); crash child also sets SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS. (2) dde402d then died 0xc0000005 twice at 630/797 right after startup_task tests: startup_task.rs makes WinRT calls on threads with no COM init, borrowing the implicit MTA that taskcom/WMI threads open and close per call; when the last closed it, the windows crate's cached activation factories pointed into a torn-down apartment. keep_mta_alive() = CoIncrementMTAUsage once before any WinRT call; deterministic child test reproduces the sequence. The desktop app runs the same readers on its thread pool, so this was a latent app crash too. (3) timeout-minutes on 12 ci.yml and 11 release.yml jobs (~3x the slowest recent run).
decision: MiniDumpWriteDump suspends every other thread of the process it dumps (Microsoft documents calling it from another process). CoIncrementMTAUsage is the documented way to keep the MTA alive for code that relies on the implicit MTA; the cookie is never released because the cached factories live until exit.

Mechanism that finally worked, after the first two attempts proved nothing: the ssh session there is ELEVATED, so the standard-user session has to be a scheduled task, and Start-Process from the ssh shell cannot launch a GUI at all (session 0, no desktop - the first SEC-7 attempt produced an empty pid for exactly that reason). vb-limited.ps1 registers the inner script with -RunLevel Limited -LogonType Interactive and Start-ScheduledTask; that is a genuine filtered token (the log prints elevated=False and the SID), and vb-elevated.ps1 registered -RunLevel Highest when the other direction was needed. The rule is location plus ACL (taskmgr.rs ensure_hook_target_is_admin_only), and a per-user install is outside Program Files by definition, so this is the honest shape of the check for a per-user build. (2) SEC-9 VERIFIED: netstat -ano for the app pid reads TCP 192.168.100.104:7331 LISTENING and TCP 127.0.0.1:7330 LISTENING, with zero listeners on 0.0.0.0 - the adapter chosen in the panel was Ethernet 3 - 192.168.100.104. (3) SEC-3 VERIFIED, with a correction to the row wording: the guard is loopback-only by design. POST /api/v1/pair on 127.0.0.1:7330 with Origin: https://evil.example returned 403 {"error":"invalid pairing code"}, with Host: evil.example returned 403, with both returned 403, and the CONTROL (no Origin, loopback Host) returned 400 "expected {code: 123456}" - so the 403s came from pair_guard, not from a wrong code. The same request to the LAN listener with a foreign Origin returned 400, i.e. NOT refused: over the network the code itself is the defence, which is what pair_guard comment says. The row says "from a browser on another host", which describes the threat as remote; the code refuses a browser on THIS host (DNS rebinding included). (4) SEC-7 HALF VERIFIED: an ELEVATED CLI attached to the UNELEVATED app - "source: attached to Vitals 1.3.0 over vitals-vladu". The reverse direction attached too, but NOT over the pipe: with the app running elevated the unelevated CLI read "source: attached to Vitals 1.3.0 on :7330", i.e. it fell back to the loopback API, so the pipe half of that direction is unproven. (5) SEC-2 PARTIAL: C:\Program Files\Vitals Sensors\install.log exists and nothing named install.log appears under the per-user install dir, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Vitals, %TEMP% or the scratch dir; but the sensors helper now REFUSES to install - "install failed: PawnIO not installed (pass --pawnio-setup <PawnIO_setup.exe 2.2.0>)" exit 3 - so the 1 MB cap and the fresh-write location were not exercised this session. STILL OPEN: the four screenshot/video captures, the phone and TV pairing (blocked twice over: the laptop has two inbound BLOCK firewall rules for vitals-desktop.exe, and its Wi-Fi carries an APIPA address while the listener is on the 192.168.100.104 adapter), and SEC-2 with PawnIO.RESOLVED 2026-11-19 (second vivobook pass, same session; the mechanism is now a script, scripts/vivobook-pass.ps1). (2) SEC-2 NOW FULLY VERIFIED: PawnIO_setup.exe 2.2.0 was downloaded and its sha256 1F519A22E47187F70A1379A48CA604981C4FCF694F4E65B734AAA74A9FBA3032 matched the pinned value; "vitals-sensors install --pawnio-setup" exited 0, PawnIO 2.2.0.0 is registered, the vitals-sensors service was created and is Running/Automatic, and a real reading came back: {"v":1,"ok":true,"vendor":"intel","packageC":64.0,"hottestCoreC":64.0,"tjMaxC":100,"packageW":null,"source":"pawnio"}. The 1 MB cap was EXERCISED rather than assumed: install.log was pre-grown to 1238490 bytes and the same run left it at 425 bytes (truncate-on-open, LOG_CAP_BYTES). Exactly one install.log exists, inside Program Files\Vitals Sensors; none under %TEMP%, the per-user install directory or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Vitals. (3) SEC-7 CORRECTED, not merely left unproven. An elevated CLI does attach to an unelevated app over the pipe ("source: attached to Vitals 1.3.0 over vitals-vladu"), but the REVERSE direction is REFUSED: an unelevated CLI forced to the pipe ("--source app", which cannot fall back) fails with "Access is denied. (os error 5)", and in the default mode it falls back to "source: attached to Vitals 1.3.0 on :7330". The cause is the pipe own descriptor, D:P(A;;GA;;;SY)(A;;GA;;;BA)(A;;GA;;;OW): an elevated token default owner is the Administrators group, so OW admits the elevated caller, not the filtered token. That is the safe direction - an unelevated process must not drive an elevated one - and the loopback API still serves it, so no code change is warranted; the claim in this row was what was wrong. (1) SEC-1, (4) SEC-9 and (5) SEC-3 remain verified. Remaining, and not this row own: the four screenshot/video captures and a phone/TV pairing - both tracked on S24-16 and both needing the owner devices.

title: Suspended-state test waits for a started child; release 1.0.5 (S21-01..07)
detail: Flaky actions::process::tests::a_suspended_process_is_reported_suspended_so_the_menu_can_offer_resume (1 in 40 full-suite runs at 16 threads, jobs 20261018-091913-8d08 and 092404-cd4c, 'a paused process must read as suspended'). title: Android signing step reports every failure; release 1.0.6 (first published build of 1.0.5)

title: Storage: weekly safe clean-up per drive (opt-in), idle + mains, catch-up at next start, toast + history
detail: Off by default; switched on per drive in the clean-up wizard (day + half-hour slot, default Sunday 03:00) and kept in settings.driveCleanupSchedules keyed by the volume GUID path (GetVolumeNameForVolumeMountPointW; letter:<X:> fallback), so a changed letter keeps it. The schedule stores when; what = the drive profile (driveCleanupProfiles) or every schedulable kind without one, filtered in Rust by drive_cleanup::schedule::schedulable: available && Safe && default_selected && !needs_elevation && !stops_wsl && !stops_docker && kind in SCHEDULABLE_KINDS (tempOld, npm/pnpm/nuget caches, docker build cache + old images, distro apt/dnf/journal/tmp/docker prune) && an exhaustive action whitelist (Compact, Sparse, Managed, HiberfilOrphan, RecycleBin, PnpmPrune, Artefact, container/volume removal = never). When: schedule::decide - due once per slot (Slot::latest on the local clock via FileTimeToLocalFileTime), settled = max(last scheduled run, enabledAt); runs when idle >= 10 min (input::idle_secs) on mains, or on mains after waiting 24 h (owner choice); never on battery or unknown line with a battery; never while the session ends; a slot missed by < 7 days runs once at the next start. Runs on a vitals-drive-schedule thread (5-min checks; same plain-thread pattern as the S21-05 idle updater), claims the wizard slots (devclean Busy + inventory managed) so it never overlaps a user run, re-analyses, intersects, and with nothing to do records a silent zero-item run. detail: New vitals-store module drive_history (its own drive-history.sqlite, always on: volume totals and clean-up sizes, not machine activity; PRIVACY.md row EN+RO). title: Per-machine copies get a prompt, a tray badge and a one-click move to per-user
detail: P0-1. When UpdatePlan::NeedsApproval and a verified download is ready: toast once per 24 h (Vitals X is ready - Restart to update asks for administrator), tray icon badge + tooltip, Settings > About shows updater status (last check, last error, mode, suppressedBy env/setting/packaged = new get_update_status), and a Move to my account action that runs the per-user setup /CurrentUser then removes the all-users copy on the next idle install. idle_secs on macOS via CGEventSourceSecondsSinceLastEventType so Macs install while idle too. Watchdog logs the version gap daily and nudges with a toast when the app is not running (launch --hidden).
decision: Owner 2026-11-12 D3: notification + badge + one-click move; no elevated scheduled task.
verification: Part 1 VERIFIED 2026-11-17 (b4ef52e + 4919ef2): get_update_status returns the pending version, the install mode, the last check, the last error and why checks are suppressed, and UpdateSuppressed is recorded at launch and unit-tested for precedence; the About panel shows one muted line in both locales, with the clock read once in the effect because the React Compiler rejects Date.now() in render; clippy Ok(()) fixed. Local: check-drift 0 failures 0 warnings, desktop lint and typecheck exit 0. Open: the once-a-day toast on NeedsApproval, the tray text beside the badge, the one-click move to a per-user install, macOS idle detection through CGEventSourceSecondsSinceLastEventType, and the watchdog nudge. Those change what the app does to its own files, so the row's own done-means - update-proof.yml 1.1.0 -> 1.3.0 unelevated on a real machine, and a run on vivobook - is what would prove them, and it needs published 1.3.0 artifacts.Part 2a DONE 2026-11-18 (34fddc1): a once-a-day toast when an update waits for approval (updates::prompt, a file-backed timestamp, 4 tests including the clock-moved-backwards case), and the tray tooltip now carries 'update X ready' so the badge is explained in words rather than guessed at. macOS idle detection added (crates/vitals-macos/src/input.rs, CGEventSourceSecondsSinceLastEventType) - before it, a Mac never reached the idle branch at all; the one gap is left visible in the code: macOS has no cheap answer for 'session ending' without AppKit, so that stays false there. Part 2b DONE 2026-11-18 (4bdbdae): 'Move Vitals to my account' in Settings > About for a per-machine copy - it writes the downloaded setup beside the app's data, sets __COMPAT_LAYER=RunAsInvoker, starts it with /CurrentUser only (never both scope switches, which a test asserts), and exits; the migration arms a marker so the next launch reports the old all-users copy for removal, which is the half that would otherwise leave two installations and say nothing. 4 pure tests for the decision table, 3 for the argument assembly, 2 component tests for when the offer appears, plus the extended leftover() cases. Verified: 887 vitals-win tests, 1379 desktop tests, check-drift 0 failures 0 warnings with 128 invokes = 128 commands (so the new command is reached from the UI), clippy -D warnings clean on vitals-win and vitals-desktop. Part 2c DONE 2026-11-18 (a997808): the watchdog half. apps/watchdog/src/version.rs reads the latest release tag from GitHub's API over WinHTTP (so no TLS stack, no async runtime and no new dependency in a process that must start in milliseconds), compares it with its own CARGO_PKG_VERSION - which IS the installed app version, because both binaries come from one release - and sends a toast through the channel the action workers already use, so the binary keeps exactly one notification path. It never acts: nothing is downloaded and nothing is installed from there, which is what the ADR requires. 9 pure tests: 1.10.0 vs 1.9.0 (the lexical trap that silently stops offering updates), a v-prefixed tag, missing components equal to zero, unparseable input reporting nothing, a pre-release suffix, and the once-a-day throttle including a clock that moved backwards. The WinHTTP path is proved live on this machine rather than assumed: an #[ignore]d test run by hand printed 'installed 1.2.0 / latest 1.2.0', so the call reads a real tag and correctly finds nothing newer (cargo test -p vitals-watchdog -- --ignored --nocapture). Verified: 74 watchdog tests, clippy -D warnings clean, rustfmt clean, the strings parity test covers the new template in both locales, and CI green on a997808. CONSEQUENCE FOUND 2026-11-19, worth knowing before the workstation move is made: the one-click move to a per-user copy takes the Task Manager replacement away. taskmgr.rs refuses any hook target outside Program Files or writable by an ordinary account, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Vitals is outside by definition - proved on vivobook, where the per-user 1.3.0 copy refused with "Vitals can replace Task Manager only when it is installed for all users in Program Files; this copy runs from ...\AppData\Local\Programs\Vitals". The refusal is correct and deliberate; what is unstated is that turning the setting on and then moving the install loses it. Not changed here - recorded so the move is not a surprise.

title: MQTT with Home Assistant discovery and a read-only MCP server
detail: D5. MQTT: optional broker URL/credentials in Settings > Remote access, publishes summary + sensors + alerts with HA discovery topics (homeassistant/sensor/vitals_<host>/.../config), retained availability, QoS 1, reconnect backoff, TLS when mqtts://, off by default; docs/integrations/home-assistant.md updated. MCP: `vitals mcp` (stdio) + optional /mcp Streamable HTTP route behind a read-scope token; tools: summary, processes (top N), sensors, alerts, history(range), diagnosis; resources per machine; no control tools in v1; register in Windows MCP on-device registry when available; docs page + Claude/Copilot/Cursor config snippets.
verification: MQTT: integration test against a local broker (rumqttd in tests) asserts discovery payloads; HA dev container shows entities (screenshot). MCP: inspector session transcript listing tools and a summary call; token-less call refused. MCP and the MQTT settings screen DONE 2026-11-18. MCP: a new crate crates/vitals-mcp owns the JSON-RPC server (initialize, tools/list, tools/call, resources/list, resources/read), the six read-only tools (summary, processes with a top count, sensors, alerts, history over a range, diagnosis) and one resource per machine; `vitals mcp` serves it over stdio in apps/cli, and crates/vitals-server serves the same route at POST /mcp behind the read-scope token. There are deliberately no control tools. Verified: cargo test -p vitals-cli -p vitals-mcp -p vitals-server green (58 tests in vitals-mcp), clippy clean, and two real-process tests - apps/cli/tests/mcp_stdio.rs performs a handshake and a tool call over stdio, apps/cli/tests/serve_mcp.rs starts the actual `vitals serve` process on a port and asserts both the handshake with a token and a 401 refusal without one (which is the "token-less call refused" the row asks for). docs/integrations/mcp.md gained Claude/Copilot/Cursor snippets and docs/api/README.md the route. Settings UI: Settings > Remote access > MQTT now sets the broker (mqtt:// or mqtts://, parsed as a URL and refused with a reason), an optional username, a password in the OS secret store (Windows Credential Manager target vitals/mqtt-password, macOS Keychain), off by default, re-applied at launch, and it starts the same vitals_server::mqtt::spawn the CLI flag uses - so the setting has an effect rather than decorating a screen. The webview never sees the password and a password smuggled into the URL is refused, because the URL is written to settings.json and a password is not. 22 new frontend tests; locale parity holds. STILL OPEN in this row: the Home Assistant dev-container screenshot (no container was run) and registering in the Windows MCP on-device registry, which does not exist yet. MQTT VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL BROKER 2026-11-19 (eclipse-mosquitto in Docker on this machine, the CLI publishing at a 2 s interval, a subscriber started BEFORE the publisher so nothing was missed): 39 messages, and the retained discovery set came through exactly as Home Assistant consumes it - homeassistant/sensor/vitals_dragos/vitals_dragos_{cpu,cpu_temperature,memory,processes,alerts,battery}/config plus homeassistant/binary_sensor/vitals_dragos/vitals_dragos_problem/config, each carrying state_topic, unique_id, unit_of_measurement, the device block (identifiers, manufacturer Vitals, sw_version 1.3.0) and payload_available/payload_not_available; then live state vitals/vitals_dragos/state/summary/{cpu,memory,processes} and vitals/vitals_dragos/state/alerts/{active,problem} every 2 s, and the lifecycle ended with vitals/vitals_dragos/availability offline on shutdown. This supersedes the dev-container screenshot as far as the payloads go: what the container would render is exactly these topics. One doc defect found and fixed while reading that output (crates/vitals-mqtt/src/feed.rs): the module comment claimed a reading that cannot be measured is "neither announced to Home Assistant nor published", but publish_discovery() iterates all_specs() and announces every entity unconditionally - battery and cpu_temperature were announced on a desktop that has neither - while the state pass is value-gated. The behaviour is the right one (announcing a subset would make the two passes depend on each other and hide a sensor that appears later); the comment was wrong, and now records the real rule. STILL OPEN: the Home Assistant container itself, which needs the interactive onboarding flow. THE PAYLOAD PROOF IS NOW KEPT BY CI 2026-11-19: crates/vitals-mqtt/tests/broker.rs drives the real Publisher against a broker and asserts the discovery set (one entity per all_specs, each carrying state_topic, unique_id and the device block), the value-gated state topics, online preceding the first reading, availability ending offline, and - through a second client that connects only after shutdown, which is the only way a retain flag can be observed - that the announcements and the availability are retained while no reading is; .github/workflows/mqtt.yml runs it on every push and pull request touching the crate, against an eclipse-mosquitto service container on Linux (image pinned by digest) and aedes started in a step on Windows, and fails the job if the test ever takes its skip path. Correction to the paragraph above: the wrong comment was in crates/vitals-mqtt/src/discovery.rs, not feed.rs (feed.rs already stated the rule correctly); both the discovery.rs comment and a stale reference in topics.rs were fixed, and the module now documents the broker recipe. THE HOME ASSISTANT CONTAINER IS DONE, AND IT FOUND A REAL DEFECT, 2026-11-20: a mosquitto container and a ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable container on one Docker network, onboarding completed over the REST API (/api/onboarding/users then /auth/token - form-encoded, because a JSON body answers unsupported_grant_type), then the MQTT integration added through the config-entry flow (the broker step requires other_settings, and set_ca_cert is a select of off/auto/custom rather than a boolean). Against that real Home Assistant EVERY entity Vitals announced was refused: 'not a valid option at device.availability_topic', because discovery_payload nested availability_topic, payload_available and payload_not_available inside the device block, which Home Assistant validates against a device schema that has no availability fields - the whole announcement is discarded, so not one entity was ever created and the feature never worked against the real thing. Availability is an entity-level option; fixed in crates/vitals-mqtt/src/discovery.rs by giving DeviceInfo::block no availability argument and leaving it identity only. The more important lesson is why CI stayed green: crates/vitals-mqtt/tests/broker.rs asserted that block[availability_topic] equalled availability, so it asserted the shape Vitals had invented instead of the shape Home Assistant accepts. That assertion is now inverted into the rule - the device block must carry no availability key - and discovery.rs carries the same assertion as a unit test, so a reintroduction fails in a second without a broker. VERIFIED after the fix with the CLI rebuilt from source: Home Assistant created 15 entities for the real machine and read them live - CPU 100.0 %, memory in use 67.8 %, processes 943, active alerts 1, CPU temperature and battery unknown because a desktop cannot measure them - and all 14 sensors became unavailable within 15 s of the publisher stopping, which is the retained availability path working end to end. The retained discovery payload was read back with no publisher running and carries no device-level availability key. cargo test -p vitals-mqtt against a live mosquitto: 29 unit tests and 1 broker test green, the broker test running rather than taking its skip path. MQTT discovery had no user documentation anywhere in docs/; docs/integrations/home-assistant.md now documents the setting, the topics, the availability model and both payload rules, with the failure recorded so it is not reintroduced.

The plan is data, not a switch: adding a verb is one table entry plus one planner arm, and a test reads the generated TypeScript binding rather than a hand-kept list. title: Every implied Android hardware feature is declared optional, and three gates hold it
detail: Android marks a hardware feature REQUIRED when a permission implies it (ACCESS_WIFI_STATE -> android.hardware.wifi, CAMERA -> android.hardware.camera) unless the manifest declares it android:required=false, and Play then hides the app from the devices that lack it. The Wi-Fi follow-up fixed the two permissions; auditing the whole surface found one more: the phone CAMERA permission still made android.hardware.camera required, and android.hardware.camera.any required=false does NOT cancel it (the uses-feature reference names camera-less Chromebooks in its own Caution). The phone now declares the back camera optional, and the TV build dropped an unused android.hardware.camera.any because a TV has no camera, that build never requests CAMERA and pairing is a typed six-digit code. Still required, each with a reason: android.hardware.type.watch, android.software.leanback and android.hardware.faketouch, which is Android's default input requirement and what the phone UI genuinely needs. Three gates hold it: scripts/check-android-features.ps1 reads aapt dump badging on every built APK (the implied features are added at packaging, so no manifest contains them) and asserts two content checks - every feature the source declares optional appears as uses-feature-not-required, and every REQUIRED feature is on the per-module allowlist in scripts/android-features.json; check-drift.ps1 check 9 runs the allowlist against merged manifests already on disk, in two seconds, with no build; ManifestFeaturesTest.kt pins the phone manifest and a mirror pins the watch. The gate is wired into verify.ps1, the pre-commit hook (when a manifest is staged) and CI android-apps with -RequireBuilt -Strict. The stale watch release artefact was rebuilt with :wear:assembleRelease from a clean detached worktree.
decision: Declare android:required=false and keep the declaration, never remove one another module relies on; a feature stays required only where the app cannot run without it. The gate decides on content rather than timestamps: skipping an artefact older than its manifest was tried and removed, because a Gradle UP-TO-DATE build leaves an old timestamp on current content and a reverted edit leaves a new one on unchanged content, so the verdict was wrong in both directions. -RequireBuilt refuses to pass when there was no APK to check at all, because a check that quietly proves nothing looks green - the lesson the store-listing guard was written from.

title: The CLI's headless LAN server has no inbound firewall rule, so `vitals serve` is unreachable from the network
detail: `vitals serve` binds 0.0.0.0:7331 and prints a pairing URL, but the only inbound Allow rules are for vitals-desktop.exe; a server started by a scheduled task or a hidden process gets no firewall prompt, where the default is Block.
decision: Fix it in the product rather than in the firewall: `vitals serve` knows the address it bound and cannot keep assuming the printed URL works - either say so when the bind is not reachable, or create/request the inbound rule the way the installer does for the app. The app is the odd one out, not the CLI.
verification: Measured 2026-11-19 on dragos-vivobook, from a second host: the server was listening on 0.0.0.0:7331 and answered 200 on loopback, while `GET http://192.168.100.104:7331/api/v1/health` returned HTTP 000 until an Allow rule for `vitals.exe` was added; `Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter` listed three Allow rules for `vitals-desktop.exe` and none for `vitals.exe`. With the rule present the pair exchange returned 200 with a 43-character token; the rule was removed again afterwards. Fixed 2026-11-19. crates/vitals-win/src/firewall.rs reads the rules from HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SharedAccess\Parameters\FirewallPolicy\FirewallRules and answers Some(true)/Some(false)/None. The registry rather than netsh or Get-NetFirewallRule because the stored form is a stable key=value list, while both tools print localised labels a parser would have to guess at. apps/cli/src/commands/serve.rs prints the exact New-NetFirewallRule command when the answer is Some(false) and stays silent on None, because an unreadable key is not a finding. Prover (the repo convention for an external boundary): cargo run -p vitals-win --example prove_firewall read 1445 rules on this machine and reported 0 admitting them, which is what makes an empty read distinguishable from a real block. End-to-end on dragos-vivobook the same day: the binary run from a path with no rule printed Some(false) and then the warning with the command, while a run whose path already had an Allow rule stayed silent - correctly, because Windows auto-creates a rule when a program binds interactively, which is exactly why the task-launched CLI on that machine had none. Gates: cargo fmt -p vitals-win -p vitals-cli --check clean, clippy --all-targets -D warnings clean, 9 firewall unit tests green (two of them failed first and were the test expectations being wrong: LPort=Any names no port, so the rule is about the program beside it).

title: Every dialog is capped at a fixed length, not at a token the app redefines
detail: Owner report 2026-11-19: modals stretch too much when the window is fullscreen and should have a maximum width and height. Root cause, found by measuring rather than reading: apps/desktop/src/styles.css redefines --container-3xl (and 4xl/5xl) to 120/160/240rem for its @3xl/main container queries, and Tailwind resolves max-w-3xl through that same token - so the Settings dialog max-w-3xl was a 1920px cap, not 48rem, and on a maximised window it filled the width. It survived review because max-w-3xl reads like a 48rem cap. Fix at the primitive, packages/ui Dialog.tsx: SIZES holds explicit lengths, a new 2xl (48rem) size for Settings, DIALOG_MAX_WIDTH_REM exported as the documented ceiling, and a comment at the styles.css token block saying a cap must be a length. All 12 DialogContent call sites inherit it; the phone ActionSheet is a full-bleed bottom sheet by design and was deliberately left alone.
verification: Measured in headless Chromium against the dev server, before -> after: 1920x1080 1888 -> 768 px, 3440x900 1920 -> 768, 1280x720 1248 -> 768 (computed max-width 1920px -> 768px). Height unchanged at 544 with the primitive existing max-h-[calc(100dvh-2rem)]. New apps/desktop/e2e/dialogs.spec.ts asserts measured pixels at three viewports, that the document never scrolls, that a dialog taller than the window scrolls its body instead of pushing content off screen, and that collapsing the sidebar at 1280x720 neither clips the dialog nor scrolls the page sideways - RE-RUN HERE independently: 5 passed (29.8s), exit 0, and the passing test names carry the guarantees. Unit guard in packages/ui Dialog.test.tsx. Mutation-checked: restoring 2xl as max-w-3xl makes the unit test fail and 4 e2e tests fail with "the dialog rendered 1248px/1812px/1843px wide, past the 768px maximum". Gates: tsc 0 both packages, eslint 0, vitest ui 166 and desktop 1421 passed, playwright 170 passed, prettier clean, check-drift 0 failures. ALSO FOUND, not fixed, and unrelated to sizing: the first click on the sidebar Settings button can be lost right after startup because the dialog sits behind a dynamic import - measured ready@440 ms and dialog@1464 ms on a warm dev server, but never opened on several cold runs with 5 workers. That is a shell/startup change, not a modal one, and the e2e opener retries so the suite measures layout rather than the import.

title: The rollout gate cannot pass by skipping
detail: scripts/check-store-listing.mjs gained --require-credentials: with it, a half of the check that cannot reach its store exits 2 instead of printing SKIPPED, and both SKIPPED lines now name .github/workflows/store-listing.yml as the workflow whose contract is to do that checking. store-listing.yml calls it strictly, tees the log, and a new always() step fails the job when the log is missing or carries any SKIPPED line - mqtt.yml's own guard pattern, so a call site that quietly drops the flag still cannot pass. release.yml is deliberately unchanged: its SKIPPED is documented above the call, because the WIF credential needs id-token: write and that job runs before the owner's approval (SEC-5).
decision: Found while cutting 1.3.1. The release CI job printed SKIPPED and exited 0, so --require-full-rollout had checked nothing on the machine that ran it, and the rollout was nearly certified from a line that skipped its own subject. Not a defect in that job - the authoritative one is store-listing.yml - but the gate was readable as a pass when it was not one.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. Locally, with no store credentials: the default prints both SKIPPED lines and exits 0; the same command plus --require-credentials exits 2 with a message naming store-listing.yml; --json reports requireCredentials true, ok false, couldNotRun 2. Mutation check: with the new branch removed from a scratch copy the same command exits 0, so that branch is what fails. The workflow guard was checked the same way - the log from the default run, which exits 0, contains two SKIPPED lines, so the guard reads red on it, while a SKIPPED-free log reads green. actionlint exit 0. In CI: the Store listing workflow ran on main after the commit and succeeded, which means the strict flag found a credential, the script did not skip, and the guard step passed.

title: The discovery payload is pinned against Home Assistant, and a real Home Assistant boots in CI
detail: The 1.3.0 defect was a payload the consumer rejects while every test stayed green: availability_topic, payload_available and payload_not_available sat inside the discovery document device block, Home Assistant discarded the whole document, and nothing else validates that shape - the unit tests build it as a value and the broker test only proves delivery. crates/vitals-mqtt/tests/home_assistant.rs now asserts that every key of every discovery document is one Home Assistant accepts, at the entity level and inside the device block, against crates/vitals-mqtt/tests/fixtures/ha_discovery_keys.json, whose _provenance block records the Home Assistant version, the image digest and how the key sets were enumerated so a reviewer can re-derive them rather than trust them. A second test is gated on VITALS_HA_URL and VITALS_HA_TOKEN and proves acceptance end to end. .github/workflows/mqtt.yml gained the job MQTT (linux, real Home Assistant): Home Assistant as a digest-pinned service container alongside the existing mosquitto one, onboarded over REST, the MQTT integration added, then the crate suite, failing if no entity appears or if either gated test takes its skip path.
decision: Owner-ticked follow-up to 1.3.0 shipping an integration that had never worked. The broker alone was not enough, and the proof that it is not is that CI was green for the whole life of the defect.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20, most of it in CI. Against the real Home Assistant in Docker on this machine, cargo test -p vitals-mqtt gave 29 unit, 1 broker and 3 home_assistant tests passed, the acceptance test printing Home Assistant created sensor.vitals_on_vitals_ha_ci_cpu with state 33.5. Mutation check: with the three availability keys re-nested into the device block in a scratch copy, the new tests fail with device.availability_topic on sensor cpu is not a key Home Assistant accepts inside device; it discards the whole document and creates no entity, and the pin self-check fails with them, so neither is decorative. The scratch copy was deleted and git diff on crates/vitals-mqtt/src/ prints 0 lines. The job run: block was extracted verbatim from the YAML and replayed against a pristine Home Assistant container, which is how the required other_settings shape and the unauthenticated GET /api/onboarding readiness probe were pinned down instead of guessed. cargo fmt --all -- --check and cargo clippy -p vitals-mqtt --all-targets -- -D warnings clean; actionlint exit 0. IN CI: run 44690023064, job MQTT (linux, real Home Assistant) completed/success, so Home Assistant really booted on the runner, the integration was created and an entity appeared - the part that could not be proven locally is now proven.

title: The Play rollout claim is machine-checked rather than prose
detail: check-store-listing.mjs now asserts instead of reporting: under --require-full-rollout a stable release whose Play rollout is not at full is a failure, a SemVer pre-release at a partial fraction is explicitly not one, and versionCodes, status and userFraction are written to the GitHub step summary so 100 percent is a value in the run rather than a sentence in a log. store-listing.yml is the workflow that owns the Play credential and the check; release.yml is deliberately unchanged, because its SKIPPED is documented there - the WIF credential needs id-token: write and that job runs before the owner approves the release environment.
decision: Cutting 1.3.1 showed the only proof of a full rollout was a line a person read out of a log. The same class of claim had previously passed a gate that was skipping its own subject, so the claim and the check for it were both prose.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. Flag matrix against a stub API: no flag and no credential prints two SKIPPED lines and exits 0, which is the unchanged default release.yml depends on; --require-credentials without one exits 2; a full rollout exits 0 and writes the summary table (versionCodes 13, completed, full); a stable 1.3.1 at fraction 0.2 exits 1 with does not cover everyone; the same 0.2 as 1.3.0-rc.1 exits 0 with an explicit not-a-failure line; --json reports preRelease true and failures 0. Mutation check: with the verdict branch replaced by a constant in a scratch copy the stable-at-0.2 case exits 0, so that branch is what fails rather than something else. NOT VERIFIED: no live Play Developer API call - there is no Play credential on this machine and androidpublisher answers 403 for the ambient ADC - so the stub drove the real parsing, verdict, exit-code and summary paths, but the wire response was not read from Google.

title: The release doctor audits every surface a release must touch
detail: scripts/release-doctor.mjs prints one row per surface and exits non-zero when any is stale: every version manifest via scripts/version.ps1, the CHANGELOG section, version literals, the MSIX what's-new strings, both Play changelogs, both Apple listings, the tag and whether it is pushed, and the release's own tracker row. Its version-literal row defers to scripts/check-drift.ps1 rather than reimplementing the rule, so one implementation of that rule exists. Surfaces that need a credential or the network report UNKNOWN rather than skipping, and the exit code states whether the run was full or partial. docs/releasing.md documents it.
decision: Two releases in this repository's history went out with a stale version string in a surface nobody checked, and the project's own agent instructions state the ripple rule only as prose plus an instruction to grep for the old version by hand. The rule is now a command.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. node scripts/release-doctor.mjs --version 1.3.1 on the current tree gives 7 OK, 2 HELD, 0 STALE, 2 UNKNOWN, exit 100, which is this script's clean-but-partial code. Mutation: a scratch copy of a packaging file carrying -Version 1.3.0.0 flips the literals row to STALE and the exit to 101, and the scratch copy was deleted afterwards. The Apple rows report HELD rather than STALE when they name an older released version, which is the row a human must read and the reason the two listing files were deliberately not moved with the bump. node --check and prettier --check clean; it is not in the pre-commit hook because at about 4 s it is heavier than the hook's target.

title: The Home Assistant key pin cannot rot silently
detail: scripts/ha-pin-refresh.mjs re-derives the accepted key sets from the current ghcr.io/home-assistant/home-assistant:stable by the same method the fixture's _provenance block records, and .github/workflows/ha-key-pin.yml runs it in --check mode weekly and on dispatch, failing the job and opening or updating a single issue when the pin is out of date. It does not run on push, so it cannot become a reason to ignore a red build.
decision: The 1.3.0 defect was a discovery payload Home Assistant rejected while every test stayed green. The pin that now catches it is a snapshot of a vocabulary that ships monthly, so an out-of-date pin reproduces exactly the failure mode it was written to prevent, with a green test in front of it.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 for the derivation; NOT VERIFIED in CI, which needs a push. The embedded derivation was run inside the official container and reproduced the committed fixture exactly: components.sensor 32 keys match, components.binary_sensor 30 match, device 13 match, RESULT IDENTICAL, at Home Assistant 2026.11.2 and the digest the provenance records. In --check mode against the repository fixture the script prints up to date with the same digest and exits 0. Mutation in a throwaway copy: a deleted sensor key plus a stale provenance digest exits 1, naming the key and both digests, and the write mode repairs it to output identical to the committed fixture. actionlint clean on the workflow. The workflow's GitHub behaviour (schedule, the create-versus-comment issue path, the pull step) is reasoned from the YAML and not observed. Also noted: the fixture's provenance points at a docs page that does not contain the enumeration script, so the method now lives in scripts/ha-pin-refresh.mjs itself.

title: check-drift now catches the version literals that have bitten twice
detail: scripts/check-drift.ps1 gained check 10: a four-part version literal bound to a version slot (-Version or version=) under packaging, scripts and .github/workflows must equal the current Store version, which is read from Cargo.toml directly rather than by spawning version.ps1. It found two real stalenesses the moment it ran, and both were fixed in this change: .github/workflows/msix.yml had a copyable command at 1.3.0.0 and packaging/msix/build-and-upload.ps1 an EXAMPLE at 1.2.0.0.
decision: The class rather than the instance. The MSIX usage examples have been left behind once per bump, and a literal in a comment is exactly what a person copies when they run a release, so scanning comments is the point rather than a false positive to suppress.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. Before the change the gate printed drift 0 failure(s), 0 warning(s); after it, 2 failures naming both files; after the two literals were corrected, 0 failure(s) 0 warning(s) again with the same 16 ts_rs files, 132 invokes, 132 commands and 2 locales counters. Mutations: a scratch packaging file at -Version 1.3.0.0 is named, -Version 1.3.1.1 is named (the four-part rule), and a toolchain pin, an npm pin, an action SHA, a URL containing a version number and a Windows SDK version all stay silent. Added cost measured in-process: 232 ms over 69 files, within the run-to-run noise of the gate. Deliberate exclusions are enumerated in the comment with reasons: format illustrations such as e.g. 1.3.0.0 in parameter help, and the three-part placeholder examples in the release tooling, which that tooling accepts as any version.

title: A preflight turns use-CI-instead into a decision with evidence
detail: scripts/machine-preflight.ps1 reports free space on C: and E:, CPU, RAM and the Windows commit charge, the agentq queue with who holds what and for what purpose, and a single verdict that names the binding constraint; -Json emits the same fields for a script or an agent to consume. It calls agentq's own status rather than reimplementing the gate's logic, and reports UNKNOWN rather than a guess when agentq or a measurement is absent.
decision: The decision to run gates in the cloud rather than on this workstation was being made from memory or from an ad-hoc probe. On 2026-11-20 that cost two wasted gate runs and a local verify.ps1 that had to be skipped in favour of CI; the same decision should be a number.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 on this machine. A real run reports disk, CPU, commit, three named agentq holdings with their sessions and purposes, and a verdict line; -Json parses under ConvertFrom-Json. Trap checks: with agentq off PATH it prints UNKNOWN and still reports the surfaces it could measure, exit 0, with no fabricated number; against a stubbed saturated queue it prints use CI. A defect found by running it and fixed in the same change: the verdict said process starts are not slow while quoting a probe median 18 times over its own 400 ms limit, because it trusted agentq's saturated flag over its own measurement. The number now decides, and when the two disagree the reason names both and says so; both disagreement directions were exercised. It always exits 0 and is deliberately not part of verify.ps1, because a tool that fails when the machine is busy is the problem it exists to describe.

title: A release cut that is not complete is refused before anything is built or signed
detail: scripts/release-preflight.mjs fails a release when the tag disagrees with any manifest (delegating to scripts/version.ps1 so a seventh manifest is covered for free), when CHANGELOG.md has no closed dated section for that version or no fresh Unreleased heading above it, or when the tag is not annotated and reachable from the pushed default branch. It lists every problem in one run rather than stopping at the first. .github/workflows/release.yml runs it as the first step of the plan job, before plan writes any output, so a failure leaves every build, sign and publish job skipped.
decision: The 1.3.1 cut was done by hand and the order mattered. The failure this guards against is a cut that looks complete and is not - a manifest left behind, or a tag pointing at a commit whose CHANGELOG section does not exist - which nobody notices until the release notes are read weeks later.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 for the script and the workflow YAML; NOT VERIFIED as a live workflow run, because the release workflow starts on a tag push and no tag could be pushed for the test. node scripts/release-preflight.mjs --tag v1.3.1 passes on the real complete cut; --ref refs/heads/main is a documented no-op for a build-only dispatch; --tag v9.9.9 fails listing three separate problems together. Mutation: a scratch CHANGELOG.md with the [1.3.1] section removed fails with exactly that one problem named. Packaging it as a step rather than a new job is deliberate and argued in a comment: a gate that failed after plan had written its outputs would leave build and publish to run, because they gate on those outputs with !cancelled(), which suppresses the implicit success() check. actionlint is clean with -shellcheck=; the three SC2129 notes it reports are pre-existing in the play job, which was not touched.

title: The Home Assistant proof is reproducible by a person and not only by CI
detail: scripts/ha-demo.ps1 stands up a broker and a real Home Assistant from digest-pinned images, onboards Home Assistant over its REST API without a browser, adds the MQTT integration, publishes a discovery document and then prints the entities Home Assistant itself created, read back from its API. -Keep leaves the rig running and prints the URL, the credentials and a link to the entity; -Down removes only a rig this script created and refuses the owner's; -Reproduce publishes a document in the 1.3.0 shape and shows Home Assistant refusing it; -FromRelease downloads a published CLI, verifies it against the release's own SHA256SUMS.txt and expects rejection; -AssertAbsent fails when a reading this machine cannot take comes back as a number instead of unknown.
decision: Bytes arriving at the broker is a different fact from Home Assistant accepting them, and only the second one is what 1.3.0 broke. The proof lived in one agent's scratch directory and in a CI job, so a user reporting no sensors had nothing to reproduce the environment with, and neither did a future maintainer.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 on this machine. The default prove run exits 0 with seven entities read back from Home Assistant's own registry, unmeasurable readings absent rather than zero; -Json emits exactly one machine-readable document on stdout with the narration moved to stderr, which was proved by a control experiment rather than assumed; -AssertAbsent cpu exits 1 with accepted true and ok false, the case that exposed the JSON reporting what the run hoped rather than what Home Assistant did; -FromRelease v1.3.0 -ExpectRejected reproduced the shipped defect with seven not-a-valid-option-at-device.availability_topic lines and zero entities; -Down refuses an unlabelled rig, naming the owner's containers, changing nothing, exit 1. Zero containers, networks or volumes left behind and the owner's own rig untouched. NOT VERIFIED: the -FromRelease cache-reuse branch and -Force, both deliberate, and any CI run, since the mqtt.yml change is a comment only.

title: The release proves its Apple half is genuinely held
detail: scripts/check-apple-hold.mjs asserts that each Apple listing's carried version is strictly behind the version the repository is building, and names the consequence when it is not: scripts/ios-store.mjs PATCHes description, keywords, promotionalText and whatsNew onto a specific appStoreVersion, so text moved along with a version bump would be written onto the version Apple is reviewing. scripts/verify.ps1 runs it in the fast lane.
decision: Moving those two files is the natural and well-meaning result of any ripple pass, and the failure would appear in App Store Connect after Apple had read text describing a version that is not the one under review. The hold is correct today but remembered only by a human and a handoff note.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. On the current tree it passes and prints why each listing is held: the iPhone listing describes 1.3.0 and the Mac listing 1.2.0 while the app is at 1.3.1. Mutation: a scratch copy of the iPhone listing moved to 1.3.1 fails with the consequence spelled out and exit 1, with the real files untouched. The version Apple is actually reviewing is NOT knowable offline - App Store Connect is the only place that holds it, and no local file names it - so the guard enforces the hold invariant rather than claiming to know that version, and it will fail by design on the day the listing legitimately moves, so lifting the hold becomes a conscious act rather than an oversight. node --check clean, verify.ps1 parses, check-drift still reports 0 failure(s) 0 warning(s).

title: The overhead budget reports the machine load beside its number
detail: crates/vitals-win/tests/overhead.rs now prints, on every run and not only on failure, the logical processor count, the process count, the system-wide busy fraction over the sampling window and this thread's own CPU time against its wall time, which is the ratio that separates our code getting slower from the scheduler taking the CPU away. The budgets and both assertions are unchanged, and the failure message states the verdict and the caveat as two sentences, claiming a busy or a quiet machine only when the numbers support it.
decision: The test's own doc comment records a 12.8 to 19.3 ms spread on an idle machine and that a 15 ms budget failed 5 runs in 8. On 2026-11-20 verify.ps1 failed on this test on a saturated workstation, on a commit whose CI was green, and the red was briefly read as a regression. The number was never wrong; it was uninterpretable without knowing what else the machine was doing.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 for compilation and lints. cargo check -p vitals-win --tests exit 0; cargo clippy -p vitals-win --all-targets -- -D warnings exit 0, run rather than reasoned, because this crate denies expect_used, unwrap_used and a pedantic set outside tests and the risk of the new code tripping it was the one thing that could go red in CI; rustfmt --check clean. No skip, retry, ignore attribute or green-washing exit was added, and the timed spans are measured exactly as before with the two thread-time reads placed outside them. NOT VERIFIED: the release run and the on-failure wording, neither observed here, because an optimised build on an admission-saturated machine measures nothing useful. They must be read in CI, which runs the same command on a hosted runner. Known limits, documented in the code: thread times update on the roughly 15.6 ms clock tick so a thread near the 50 percent threshold can flip the caveat sentence, and a 50 percent busy threshold is optimistic on very large machines.

title: The release job could not create the release and the culprit was a field nobody suspected
detail: Publishing v1.3.1 failed at POST /releases with 403 Resource not accessible by integration while every other job was green, and a re-run failed identically, which skipped all five channel jobs. The publish job declares contents write, id-token write and attestations write, and its four attestation steps succeeded in the same run, so the permission was granted; the job is byte-identical to the one that published 1.3.0 two days earlier; the repository is public and not a fork, not archived; both tag and branch rulesets are unchanged since 2026-09-29 with the owner as their bypass actor; and git ls-remote shows the pinned 3bb12739 is v2.6.2 rather than a drifted v3. GitHub refuses a release from GITHUB_TOKEN when the request carries target_commitish and that commit's .github/workflows differs from the default branch (softprops/action-gh-release#836, comment of 2026-10-21, reproduced there with probe workflows: tag_name alone is accepted, the same body plus target_commitish is refused). A tag is cut from main, so this fires as soon as any workflow commit lands on main after the tag: 1.3.0 had none and 1.3.1 had five. The step now creates the release through gh api with no commit target, uploads the assets with gh release upload --clobber, and reads the release back so the run reports what the API stored rather than that the calls returned 0.
decision: Pinning action-gh-release to v2.6.2 in September was a partial sighting of the same bug, since every version of the action sends target_commitish, so the pin hid it until a workflow commit landed after a tag; removing the field is the fix, and the Dependabot ignore that named v3 goes with the pin. The tag exists and is authoritative, and target_commitish only means anything when a tag must be created. The recovery path, and the deliberate exception to the immutable-tag ruleset it needs, are documented in docs/releasing.md, including that a re-run cannot rescue an already-frozen tag because it uses the workflow file from the tag's own commit.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. Run 44674536062: Plan, Verify, four builds, SBOM and sign + notarise macOS succeeded, Publish failed, and npm, Google Play, winget, Scoop and Chocolatey were skipped; --log-failed names POST /releases, 403 Resource not accessible by integration and Skip retry. The same 403 returned on a re-run at 15:36:49Z, so it is deterministic rather than a GitHub blip (githubstatus reported all systems operational through it). Refutations were run rather than reasoned: the attestation steps succeeded under the same permissions block, which is the one fact the 403 appears to deny; git diff --stat of the publish job between tag v1.3.0 and v1.3.1 is empty; the repository API reports public, not a fork, not archived; both rulesets date from 2026-09-29 with the owner as bypass actor; git ls-remote maps the pin to v2.6.2. The fix's request shape was measured harmlessly with GH_DEBUG=api against an existing tag: the body carries tag_name and no target_commitish and the call returns 422 already_exists, creating nothing. actionlint -shellcheck= clean on the changed workflow; the PowerShell embedded in the step was extracted from the YAML and parsed rather than eyeballed. NOT VERIFIED: the repaired publish job itself, which can only run from a tag carrying the fix, and therefore the publication of v1.3.1, which is still withheld.

title: The release goes public only once every asset is attached
detail: scripts/release-publish.ps1 (new) creates the release as a draft, uploads every file from publish/ with gh release upload --clobber, then flips it public with a PATCH on the release id read from the create call own JSON response, and finally reads the release back and compares the stored asset names against the directory in both directions. The release workflow publish job calls it instead of carrying the inline step, and every API call checks the exit code and throws with what it means for the release state.
decision: /releases/latest resolves a draft only once it is published, so a release that goes live before its assets are attached answers 404 for as long as the upload takes, and that window is exactly one an update check can land in. Taking it public last means latest.json and the files it names appear together. The release id is parsed from the response rather than scraped from its text, so the PATCH cannot address the wrong release.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 as far as it can be without a live publish. The create call and the flip are one API call the previous step made and one it did not, and the id now comes from the create response instead of a second lookup. actionlint -shellcheck= clean on the workflow. NOT VERIFIED: the create, upload and flip sequence against the live API, which needs a tag carrying this change; the repaired step has never run.

title: A release with a missing file is a red run rather than a user failed update
detail: The same script asserts the asset set before anything is created and again against what the API stored. latest.json must be present; every file latest.json names must be in the directory and must have a .sig beside it; and the uploaded set is compared against the directory both ways, printing expected but missing and uploaded but unexpected. The signature rule reads the formats that were actually signed out of the directory rather than a hard-coded platform list, because the fixed-name copies scripts/stable-assets.ps1 writes are deliberately unsigned and a Debian package carries no updater signature at all.
decision: The failure a user sees when the manifest or a signature is missing is a failed update on every installed copy, reported by a client that cannot say why, and it is invisible to the run that uploaded the files. A platform list kept in the script would go stale silently; deriving the signed formats from the directory means a new platform needs no edit here and still fails when a signature is removed.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 by mutation, independently of the author. M1: a complete 17-file set exits 0 and prints the manifest. M2: removing the .sig of the file latest.json references fails naming it, no .sig beside Vitals_1.3.2_x64-setup.exe, Vitals_x64-setup.exe (the exit code printed in that check was read through a truncated pipeline and is not evidence; the message is). The author M3 removes an installer and M4 removes latest.json, which fails with the 404 consequence. Every run was made with GH_TOKEN unset and GH_HOST pointed at an unroutable host, so the assertions read the directory only; the -DryRun branch returns before the first gh call. It is not vacuous when nothing is signed: latest.json is the authority for what the updater fetches, and a name in it without a .sig fails.

title: Why release creation sends no commit target and what a frozen tag costs
detail: docs/adr/0045 records the 403, the four causes refuted by command rather than by reasoning, the decision to create the release through gh api with no target_commitish instead of re-pinning or vendoring the action, and the operational consequence that a re-run cannot rescue an already-frozen tag because it executes the workflow file from the tag own commit. The operator-facing recovery recipe and its single defensible window, before any release has been published against the tag, stay in docs/releasing.md; the two cross-reference each other and the ADR index lists the new record.
decision: The September pin to v2.6.2 was a partial sighting of the same bug and every version of the action sends the field, so the choice is between removing the field and hiding the cause again on the next bump. The recovery path is deliberately an exception to the immutable-tag ruleset, which is why its window is written down rather than assumed.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20. docs/adr/README.md is the only index enumerating ADRs (docs/architecture.md links to it rather than listing them) and it carries the new row. pnpm exec prettier --check is clean on the ADR, the index and docs/releasing.md. scripts/check-drift.ps1 still reports 0 failure(s), 0 warning(s).

title: The publish path can be rehearsed and cannot publish anything
detail: release.yml gains workflow_dispatch with a required tag input, and a rehearse job gated on github.event_name == workflow_dispatch while publish is gated on == push, so the create, upload and flip code is absent from a rehearsal run rather than skipped inside it. The rehearsal assembles publish/ from the same artefacts, signs the updater bundles with a throwaway key generated in the run so the assertions are the real ones, writes the same latest.json, and calls the script with -DryRun: it asserts, reports the payload and the manifest to the step summary, uploads them as an artefact and exits. It declares contents: read and no environment, so it needs no approval.
decision: A rehearsal that shared the publish job would leave the publishing calls one condition away from running, and reaching them would need the release environment approval, which is the opposite of a rehearsal. Making it a separate job removes the calls from the run instead, so the safety property is structural rather than a flag someone can flip.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-20 for everything that can be checked without dispatching a run. actionlint -shellcheck= clean; the 33 embedded pwsh steps were extracted from the YAML and parsed with no incomplete input; the four gh calls in the script all sit after the -DryRun return at line 197; the throwaway signing commands were run (tauri signer generate --ci exit 0, then sign exit 0 with the generated key). NOT VERIFIED: an actual workflow_dispatch run, which has not been started, and therefore the rehearsal end to end.

title: Processes grid: a header click sorts, expanded children land in a stable order, a trailing-space search matches
detail: Three defects the owner reported, each with its root cause. (1) Clicking a column header did nothing: the header click can only happen with the pointer over the table, so the frozen guard (hovering or keyboardInGrid or menuOpen or request !== null) was always true exactly then, and a frozen reconcile only appends new children and never reorders, so resort stayed false. An explicit request, a column or a direction change, now clears the previous order independently of frozen. (2) A newly expanded tree row appeared in feed order because it arrives through the added path and a tie compared equal, so a tie fell back to arrival order; first placement now uses a deterministic tie-break (locale Intl.Collator, numeric and case-insensitive, then PID), used only for first placement. (3) matchesQuery did not trim, so a search with a trailing space matched nothing. The End task button is now always rendered on the toolbar rather than only in the context menu, disabled until a row is selected, and routed through the same beginAction('terminate', row) then plan then confirm path as the context menu, with the reason in its title when the host cannot terminate processes. One new string toolbar.selectHint in both locales.
decision: An explicit user request outranks the frozen guard; the deterministic tie-break applies only to first placement, so a settled list is never re-ordered by it.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-24. pnpm --filter @vitals/desktop exec vitest run src/features/processes: 14 files / 151 tests passed. Three mutations proved the new tests bite and were then restored: breaking the freeze guard, the first-placement tie-break and the search trim each failed exactly the intended test. title: AI page → Resources: what each AI tool is costing the machine, attributed by recorded identity
detail: A new Resources tab, and the same section on the Overview, shows per AI tool the processes, processor, memory (working set and private), disk read and write, network and GPU plus VRAM where the driver reports it, computed by filtering the live process list, the same snapshot the Processes screen uses, deliberately not a second sampling loop because per-process CPU is a delta and a second enumeration would report 0 % everywhere. agentq is identified by its own running and suspect jobs in .codai/coord/jobs (pid and pidStart); clients by the recorded identities in coord/agents (appPid or shellPid and start times); then name rules for code, code - insiders, cursor, vscodium, claude, copilot, codex, hermes, openclaw and kodwen/codwen/codai, and a description fallback only when it names the product. Deliberately refused: node.exe, pwsh.exe, python, git, cargo, deno, bun, because node.exe hosts most npm CLIs and every build script, so claiming it would put everything compiling on the machine on an agent's bill. Recorded identity beats a name; a start time is checked with a 2 second tolerance because Windows recycles PIDs; a process is counted once, under its nearest claimed ancestor; a tool with no process gets no row; a series any contributor fails to report is null, never a partial sum.
decision: Attribute by recorded identity, never by executable name alone; refuse shared runtimes; guard PID reuse with the start time; count a process once under its nearest claimed ancestor; report null rather than a partial sum when a contributor is unmeasured (ADR-0039 point 6 amendment).

title: AI page → Resources: the agentq figure broken down into what agentq is executing
detail: The agentq row was one number for the whole process tree, so a build, a land and an install were indistinguishable and the slow one could not be named. Each row is now one piece of work agentq holds a process for: a held queue ticket (held true), a running release run (state running), or a running or suspect job, read from the same files the identity rules already used, so no new sampling was added. A row carries the kind of work derived from the resource prefix (build, commit, push, land, install, deploy) or, when a ticket holds no recognised resource, from the recorded command; a release run and a job take their kind from the record agentq wrote, deploy and job, because their purpose and command are prose or an inline script path and matching those named the file rather than the work (a job waiting for a freeze to clear read as a land because its script is called land-when-unfrozen.ps1), with a test-run marker (cargo test, cargo nextest, nextest run, vitest, pytest, pnpm test, npm test, yarn test, gradlew test, gate-run) ranking above the prefix and the command; the label; the resource; the repository; the purpose and the command; the session that queued it; the pid; the start time; and the same measurements a client row carries. The rows are folded from the same process table in the same pass as the agentq figure, so they are exactly that figure partitioned, and a test asserts the identity rather than trusting it. A claim needs a recorded start time matching within the 2 second tolerance, so a stale entry or a recycled pid claims nothing; a dead holder is excluded on purpose, because the question is what is running and costing now. Later claims win, so the shell a client queued a build through is agentq's while the editor keeps its own process, and a process nobody recorded stays with the client that started it, which the panel states in its own footnote. Leases are deliberately not claimed, because a lease pid is the creating session and claiming it would steal the client row. Work that owns no process gets no row, rows are sorted busiest first, and the panel keys each row by its pid so two rows holding the same resource name cannot collide.
decision: The breakdown has to be the same measurement rather than a second opinion: the work rows and the agentq total are folded in one pass, so they cannot disagree, and a test asserts the identity. Every claim requires a recorded start time within the 2 second tolerance, so a recycled pid can never be charged. Dead holders are excluded, because the question is what is running and costing now. The later, more specific claim wins, so a queued build is agentq's while the editor keeps its own process. A lease is never claimed, because its pid is the creating session. The kind comes from agentq's own record and never from a process name or from prose: the resource prefix of a held ticket, the recorded command of a ticket whose resource names no kind, and deploy or job for the two records that are one by definition, so a release run or a job cannot be renamed by the words in a purpose or a script path (ADR-0039 point 6 amendment).

detail: A duplicate-key warning naming Vitals was reported from the console. It was chased by attaching to the running window over the WebView2 DevTools protocol with scripts/cdp-console.mjs, which prints every console line with its component stack and proves its own subscription is live by emitting a line and requiring it back. title: AI page: an ETA and a progress bar on every agentq work row
detail: Every row under Resources -> What agentq is running now carries a progress bar and the time it has left. The estimate is agentq's own measurement rather than a model: every `done` event in its journal records how many seconds that run took, so a new WorkProfiles cache, shared per coord root with the journal tail that already parses those events, keeps the last forty durations of each resource token and answers with their median - for a ticket, the resource the ticket holds; for a release, the `deploy:<repo>:<target>` it holds; and for a background job, the figure its launcher declared with `job-start.ps1 -ExpectMin`, which is the same number agentq already compares a running job against to call it suspect at twice it. `AgentqWorkUsage.estimate` carries the duration from the work's first moment together with which of the two figures it is and how many runs stand behind it, so the bar and the sentence beside it are two readings of one duration and cannot disagree as the clock moves. A resource agentq has never finished yields no estimate and the row draws no bar at all, rather than a bar at zero. Profiles survive journal rotation, because a rotation says nothing about what a resource costs.
decision: Measured where a measurement exists, declared where a launcher promised one, absent where neither - an estimate invented from a resource name would read exactly like a known one. Median rather than mean, and at most forty runs per resource: a build's duration is a distribution with a long tail that one pathological run would otherwise move. The bar is scaled against the whole expected duration rather than normalised per row, so rows stay comparable with each other. The basis travels with the number, because an overrun of a launcher's promise and an overrun of a resource's usual cost are different news, and the row says which in the same sentence a screen reader is given as the value. `aria-valuenow` is clamped to the expected duration, since a value above `aria-valuemax` is an invalid state a screen reader may refuse to read, and the overrun lives in the text beside the bar instead.

title: Every gate but one runs on the devcloud, a repository declares what its lanes need, and a lane that never returned now returns
detail: This workstation runs several agents at once, so the twenty minutes scripts/verify.ps1 took here were twenty minutes of CPU the agents competed with; the same gates take about two on an idle machine, which is the real cost. Windows lanes are now submitted to the devcloud workspace ws-vitals-win as their own agentq jobs (-Where auto is the default, -Where local and AGENTQ_WHERE=local are the way out, AGENTQ_CLOUD_STRICT=1 removes the fallback so a run that happened here cannot be mistaken for one that did not), and the Linux clippy lane stays on ws-codai because vitals-core has to keep compiling where vitals-win does not exist. A cloud lane is this same script invoked as -Lane <name> -Where local, so a gate is defined once and the boundary carries a name; each lane prints LANE_RESULT|<lane>|<gate>|<pass|fail>|<seconds> and the caller rebuilds the same table from those lines, with a row for a lane that died before reaching a gate rather than a silent absence. The android artefact lane moved too: the workspace now carries Temurin JDK 21 and the Android SDK 37 under C:\devcloud-tools, installed by an idempotent scripts/ci/provision-cloud-workspace.ps1 that writes env.ps1 for a job shell that predates the variables, and the cloud submission passes -RequireAndroid so a workspace that lost its toolchain fails loudly instead of answering nothing to check and certifying nothing. Every lane this repository runs is declared in .devcloud/profile.json (toolchains, machine class, how many jobs may share it, how long it may take, and why for the two claims a reader cannot re-derive), validated against the schema and against the families that exist live by the repository that owns the images. Two readers were waiting for a toolchain daemon instead of for their job, and one of them is why this lane never returned: (1) the workspace agent ended a step when its process exited AND its output pipes closed, and Gradle daemon on Windows outlives its client by hours, so the step never settled and no result.json was ever written - agentq commit 51308e8 settles on process exit with half a second to drain, deployed by writing the instance metadata key runner-agent; (2) the lane itself invoked each gate script block and consumed its pipeline, which also ends on EOF, so the same daemon held the lane open - measured locally on 2026-11-25 at 41 s for a gate that had finished in 0.2 s, and on the devcloud it is indistinguishable from a hang because the runner waits for the lane. Each gate now runs as its own process with its output in files and a 30-minute deadline that kills the tree and turns a gate that never returns into a red one. The blind spot underneath both: a devcloud job only publishes output when one of its children speaks, and a redirect makes a long step invisible, so scripts/lib/devcloud-progress.ps1 appends a timestamped phase line to jobs/<id>/stage in the jobs bucket and both the lane and the gate use it - before it existed, eleven minutes of a hung assemble were diagnosed from the instance CPU graph. Separately, the weekly image rebake was comparing nothing: the deployed scheduler body had six steps and a 6000 s timeout while the repository declared eight and 9000 s, so rust-tauri-win (1006 h) and win-desktop (945 h) had never been rebaked and the newest families were not in it at all. The body was re-posted and the comparison is now a script (vmui c1b2d4aa: infra/devcloud/images/check-schedule-drift.ps1, reachable as images.ps1 -VerifySchedule) that names every step, the timeout and each difference instead of trusting a schedule to be what the file says. The caller had a defect of its own, and running the whole set is what found it: it ended every cloud lane in one opaque row, because the cloud client narrates through [Console]::Out.WriteLine - the process's own stdout and not a PowerShell stream - so called in-process its log never reached the pipeline that parses LANE_RESULT. It is invoked as a child process now, and seconds are rendered invariantly rather than through the caller's culture, which had printed the same measurement as 1,1s beside a remote 15.60.
decision: Placement is a parameter of the gate with the local machine as its fallback rather than its default, and the only thing that crosses the machine boundary is a lane name, because a second copy of the gate list would drift and a sync failure that looks like a pass is worse than a slow lane. A lane waits for its gate process and never for its pipes: an end defined by a closed pipe belongs to whoever holds the other end, which in this repository is a Gradle daemon, and the same rule was learned twice at two levels before it was written down. A gate that cannot check anything is a failure, not a skip, which is why the cloud lane is submitted with -RequireAndroid and why the default for the android lane is on now that the workspace has the toolchain that makes the answer honest. A job narrates its own phases to the job prefix, because from outside a working gate and a wedged one are the same picture: no lines, low CPU, no network. What a lane needs is declared in the repository and validated against the images that exist (vmui owns the schema; the placement that consumes the profile is still not implemented, and docs/devcloud.md says so rather than implying it).

title: Agent collaboration page: who is present, what they asked each other and what is running
detail: A new page, AI agents -> Collaboration, reads %USERPROFILE%\.codai\coord read-only and shows three things: the agents registered there with their repository, their verb and their last call (live = seen within 30 minutes, the same window `agentq-msgs.ps1` Get-LiveAgents uses), every conversation in `msgs/` as a question with its answers nested under it and the newest exchange first, and the work in flight from `jobs/` with the running rows before the finished ones. New module `crates/vitals-agents/src/collab.rs` (read-only by construction: every `fs::write` in the file is inside the test module), `examples/prove_collab.rs` to run it against a real machine, the `CollabSnapshot`/`Agent`/`Sender`/`Answer`/`Thread`/`Job` types in vitals-core with their ts-rs bindings, the `get_collab` command in apps/desktop/src-tauri, and the screen itself with a 4 s poll while it is visible and a 1 s clock for the elapsed times. Navigation gains a fourteenth route, `collab`, and `e2e/support.ts` a matching row. A figure that cannot be measured is absent rather than zero: a registry entry that was never seen has no last-seen time and the page draws an em dash, a thread with no message in it is dropped instead of shown empty, and a job that finished more than 24 h ago is not listed at all.
decision: Read the channel agentq already writes rather than build a new one: the agents on this machine answer exactly these three questions there, `agentq-msgs.ps1` has written that shape for months, and a daemon RPC or codai's Postgres would each add a trust boundary or a network dependency to a page that is local. Read-only on purpose - a viewer that can post into the channel agents coordinate through is a way to corrupt coordination from a UI, and every agentq write already goes through its queue. The 30-minute liveness window is taken from Get-LiveAgents so the page and the tools cannot disagree about who is present; the 24 h windows keep a stale registry from reading as news. Polling while visible rather than watching the directory, because it is small and a file watcher on another program's scratch folder is a liability. ADR-0049 records this choice; ADR-0039 is its parent - the same page family and the same read-only rule. The cloud half, agents running in Codwen's cloud appearing in the same view, is deliberately NOT decided here.
verification: VERIFIED 2026-11-25 on this workstation. cargo clippy -p vitals-agents -p vitals-core --all-targets -- -D warnings exit 0 (36.9 s); cargo test -p vitals-agents -p vitals-core exit 0 (25.6 s, 85 tests in vitals-agents); cargo run -q -p vitals-agents --example prove_collab exit 0 (4 s), printing 9 present of 618 agents, 3 threads, 325 jobs (12 running) against this machine's real coordination directory; vitest run src/features/agents exit 0 (8 files, 61 tests); pnpm typecheck exit 0 (10.3 s); scripts/check-drift.ps1 exit 0 (9.9 s, 0 failure, 0 warning, 16 ts_rs files, 135 invokes, 135 commands, 2 locales). Two defects were found by opening the page, not by a unit test, and both are fixed: the counts reached the screen as the literal placeholders {{present}} and {{running}}, and the e2e fake host answered neither get_collab nor show_main_window.
